# The question and the analysis

How can we estimate treatment differences at a final visit and across several
visits, while accounting for baseline measurements and incomplete follow-up?
This example uses the artificial `fev_data` shipped with `mmrm` to illustrate a
hypothetical two-arm randomized trial. It is an analysis recipe, not evidence
about a real treatment. Familiarity with the [package introduction](introduction.html)
is assumed.

We treat `FEV1_BL` as a measurement collected before treatment and `VIS1` to
`VIS4` as categorical follow-up visits. The response is `FEV1`; differences
are expressed on its original scale. The participant is the independent
sampling unit. For the randomized population represented by these artificial
data, our two illustrative targets are:

- the treatment minus placebo mean difference at `VIS4`;
- the equally weighted average of the treatment minus placebo differences at
  `VIS3` and `VIS4`.

The second target gives each visit weight one half, irrespective of how many
responses are observed there. These contrasts should be specified before
looking at results. A real trial also needs an explicit strategy for
intercurrent events, such as treatment discontinuation, which these data do
not provide.

We compare two Gaussian models fitted by restricted maximum likelihood (REML),
with an unstructured within-participant covariance and Satterthwaite degrees
of freedom:

1. A **baseline-adjusted MMRM** models follow-up responses conditional on baseline,
   with a separate baseline slope at each visit and a common slope across arms.
2. A **constrained longitudinal data analysis (cLDA)** includes baseline in the
   response vector and constrains its population mean to be the same in both
   arms. Follow-up means remain separate for each arm and visit.

Randomization motivates the common population baseline mean; it does not make
the observed baseline means identical. This constraint is not automatically
appropriate for an observational comparison. The joint cLDA model also models
the distribution of baseline, whereas the baseline-adjusted model conditions
on its observed value. See [Liu et al. (2009)](https://doi.org/10.1002/sim.3639),
[Lu (2010)](https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1541-0420.2009.01332.x), and
[Coffman et al. (2016)](https://doi.org/10.1136/bmjopen-2016-013096).

# Prepare one baseline record per participant

```{r data, message = FALSE}
library(mmrm)
library(emmeans)

post <- fev_data
subjects <- unique(post[c("USUBJID", "ARMCD", "FEV1_BL")])
stopifnot(
  !anyDuplicated(subjects$USUBJID),
  !anyDuplicated(post[c("USUBJID", "AVISIT")]),
  !anyNA(subjects)
)
```

`FEV1_BL` is repeated across follow-up records. Taking distinct participant,
arm, and baseline combinations checks that those copies agree. The helper
below creates exactly one baseline response per participant, including those
whose first follow-up response is missing. It deliberately keeps the baseline
covariate out of the cLDA data: baseline enters that model only as a response.

```{r prepare-long}
make_long <- function(data) {
  baseline <- unique(data[c("USUBJID", "ARMCD", "FEV1_BL")])
  stopifnot(
    !anyDuplicated(baseline$USUBJID),
    !anyDuplicated(data[c("USUBJID", "AVISIT")])
  )
  baseline$FEV1 <- baseline$FEV1_BL
  baseline$AVISIT <- "VIS0"
  columns <- c("USUBJID", "ARMCD", "AVISIT", "FEV1")
  long <- rbind(baseline[columns], data[columns])
  long$AVISIT <- factor(long$AVISIT, levels = paste0("VIS", 0:4))
  cell_levels <- c(
    "Baseline",
    paste(rep(c("PBO", "TRT"), each = 4), paste0("VIS", 1:4), sep = "_")
  )
  long$CELL <- factor(
    ifelse(long$AVISIT == "VIS0", "Baseline", paste(long$ARMCD, long$AVISIT, sep = "_")),
    levels = cell_levels
  )
  long[order(long$USUBJID, long$AVISIT), ]
}

long <- make_long(post)
with(long, table(AVISIT, observed = !is.na(FEV1)))
```

The helper is specific to this two-arm, four-follow-up example. For another
study, adapt and validate the visit and treatment levels before using it.
Missing responses remain missing; no imputation has been performed.

# Encode and check the common baseline mean

`CELL` has one shared baseline level and eight arm-by-follow-up levels.
With no intercept, its nine coefficients are exactly the nine model means.
`AVISIT` remains a factor and specifies the covariance structure.

```{r design}
design <- model.matrix(~ 0 + CELL, data = long)
baseline_design <- design[long$AVISIT == "VIS0", , drop = FALSE]
stopifnot(
  ncol(design) == 9L,
  qr(design)$rank == 9L,
  nrow(unique(baseline_design)) == 1L
)
unique(data.frame(long[c("AVISIT", "ARMCD", "CELL")], row.names = NULL))
```

Inspecting the design matrix matters. Simply omitting an `ARMCD` main effect
from `AVISIT + AVISIT:ARMCD` does not impose the desired baseline constraint
when visit is a factor. Replacing visit by a numeric variable would instead
restrict the time trend. The cell-means construction avoids both problems.

```{r fit}
fit_clda <- mmrm(
  FEV1 ~ 0 + CELL + us(AVISIT | USUBJID),
  data = long, reml = TRUE, method = "Satterthwaite"
)
fit_adjusted <- mmrm(
  FEV1 ~ ARMCD * AVISIT + FEV1_BL * AVISIT + us(AVISIT | USUBJID),
  data = post, reml = TRUE, method = "Satterthwaite"
)
stopifnot(
  component(fit_clda, "convergence") == 0L,
  component(fit_adjusted, "convergence") == 0L
)
```

The `FEV1_BL * AVISIT` term allows baseline adjustment to differ by visit.
Using only a common baseline slope would add a restriction absent from the
unstructured joint cLDA model. The latter estimates a five-by-five covariance
matrix, including baseline; the conditional model estimates a four-by-four
covariance matrix for follow-up. Sparse data can make either difficult to
estimate. Convergence alone does not validate the mean or covariance model.

# Obtain the planned contrasts with `emmeans`

`CELL` already defines the allowable means. We request those means directly
and set `nesting = NULL` to disable automatic nesting detection. Although
`AVISIT` determines the covariance, no additional averaging over it changes
the mean associated with a given cell.

```{r contrasts}
cell_means <- emmeans(fit_clda, ~CELL, nesting = NULL)
cell_table <- as.data.frame(cell_means)

planned_weights <- function(cells) {
  list(
    final_visit = as.numeric(cells == "TRT_VIS4") - as.numeric(cells == "PBO_VIS4"),
    average_last_two = (
      as.numeric(cells %in% c("TRT_VIS3", "TRT_VIS4")) -
        as.numeric(cells %in% c("PBO_VIS3", "PBO_VIS4"))
    ) / 2
  )
}

weights <- planned_weights(as.character(cell_table$CELL))
knitr::kable(data.frame(CELL = cell_table$CELL, weights), row.names = FALSE)
planned <- contrast(cell_means, method = weights)
results <- as.data.frame(summary(planned, infer = c(TRUE, TRUE), adjust = "none"))
display_results <- results
display_results$p.value <- format.pval(results$p.value, digits = 3, eps = 0.001)
knitr::kable(display_results, digits = 3, row.names = FALSE)
```

Weights are matched by cell labels, rather than assumed row positions. For
the average, `emmeans` propagates the covariance between the two visit-specific
differences; averaging their standard errors would be incorrect. Positive
estimates indicate higher mean `FEV1` on treatment. Whether that difference
is clinically important requires context absent from this artificial example.

These are individual 95% confidence intervals. If both contrasts form one
confirmatory family, an analysis plan must address multiplicity. For example,
Bonferroni-adjusted intervals and tests for this two-contrast family are:

```{r multiplicity}
summary(planned, infer = c(TRUE, TRUE), adjust = "bonferroni", by = NULL)
```

This adjustment is across the two requested contrasts, not across separate
visit groups. It does not correct for additional analyses selected after
examining the data.

# What changes when baseline is missing?

For illustration, we remove baseline for 40 participants selected at random.
This imposed baseline missingness is missing completely at random (MCAR).
It says nothing about the mechanism behind the missing follow-up values
already present in `fev_data`. We overwrite **all** copies of each selected
participant's baseline before constructing the long data.

```{r missing-baseline}
set.seed(448)
missing_ids <- sample(as.character(subjects$USUBJID), size = 40L)
missing_post <- post
missing_post$FEV1_BL[missing_post$USUBJID %in% missing_ids] <- NA_real_
missing_long <- make_long(missing_post)

fit_clda_missing <- mmrm(
  FEV1 ~ 0 + CELL + us(AVISIT | USUBJID),
  data = missing_long, reml = TRUE, method = "Satterthwaite"
)
fit_adjusted_missing <- mmrm(
  FEV1 ~ ARMCD * AVISIT + FEV1_BL * AVISIT + us(AVISIT | USUBJID),
  data = missing_post, reml = TRUE, method = "Satterthwaite"
)

adjusted_rows <- complete.cases(missing_post[c("FEV1", "FEV1_BL", "ARMCD", "AVISIT", "USUBJID")])
common_ids <- unique(missing_post$USUBJID[adjusted_rows])
fit_clda_common <- mmrm(
  FEV1 ~ 0 + CELL + us(AVISIT | USUBJID),
  data = missing_long[missing_long$USUBJID %in% common_ids, ],
  reml = TRUE, method = "Satterthwaite"
)

fits <- list(
  "Original cLDA" = fit_clda,
  "Original adjusted MMRM" = fit_adjusted,
  "Missing baseline: cLDA" = fit_clda_missing,
  "Missing baseline: adjusted MMRM" = fit_adjusted_missing,
  "Missing baseline: cLDA, common participants" = fit_clda_common
)
stopifnot(all(vapply(fits, function(fit) component(fit, "convergence") == 0L, logical(1))))
populations <- data.frame(
  analysis = names(fits),
  participants = vapply(fits, function(fit) component(fit, "n_subjects"), numeric(1)),
  observed_responses = vapply(fits, function(fit) component(fit, "n_obs"), numeric(1))
)
knitr::kable(populations, row.names = FALSE)
```

The response counts include baseline for cLDA and only follow-up for the
adjusted model. Even before the imposed deletions, three participants have
baseline but no observed follow-up; only cLDA uses their data. After deletion,
the adjusted model also excludes every participant with missing baseline,
whereas cLDA can use their observed follow-up responses. A participant with
no observed response at any visit contributes to neither model.

To compare estimates as well as counts, we use the same weights for each
model. In the adjusted model, arm differences do not depend on the baseline
value used by the reference grid because there is no arm-by-baseline
interaction.

```{r compare}
contrast_results <- function(fit, joint) {
  if (joint) {
    means <- emmeans(fit, ~CELL, nesting = NULL)
    cells <- as.character(as.data.frame(means)$CELL)
  } else {
    means <- emmeans(fit, ~ ARMCD * AVISIT)
    grid <- as.data.frame(means)
    cells <- paste(grid$ARMCD, grid$AVISIT, sep = "_")
  }
  as.data.frame(summary(
    contrast(means, method = planned_weights(cells)),
    infer = c(TRUE, TRUE), adjust = "none"
  ))
}

comparison <- do.call(rbind, lapply(seq_along(fits), function(i) {
  cbind(analysis = names(fits)[i], contrast_results(fits[[i]], joint = i %in% c(1, 3, 5)))
}))
knitr::kable(
  comparison[c("analysis", "contrast", "estimate", "SE", "lower.CL", "upper.CL")],
  digits = 3, row.names = FALSE
)
```

The cLDA analysis on the common participants helps separate differences in
who is analyzed from differences between the fitted models. It is a
diagnostic comparison, not an alternative primary analysis chosen for its
result. We do not expect exact agreement between these REML fits with
incomplete data, and this one example does not establish bias, coverage,
power, or superiority of either method.

```{r plot, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 5, fig.alt = "Treatment minus placebo estimates with individual 95 percent confidence intervals for each model and analysis population, separately for the final visit and the average of the last two visits."}
library(ggplot2)
comparison$analysis <- factor(comparison$analysis, levels = rev(names(fits)))
ggplot(comparison, aes(x = estimate, y = analysis)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = 2, color = "grey60") +
  geom_segment(aes(x = lower.CL, xend = upper.CL, yend = analysis)) +
  geom_point() +
  facet_wrap(~contrast, ncol = 1, labeller = as_labeller(c(
    final_visit = "Final visit", average_last_two = "Average of the last two visits"
  ))) +
  labs(x = "Treatment minus placebo (FEV1 scale; individual 95% CI)", y = NULL) +
  theme_bw(base_size = 10)
```

# Check the numerical calculation

For these cell means, build the contrast matrix explicitly in coefficient
order. Estimates and standard errors must agree with $L\hat\beta$ and
$\sqrt{\operatorname{diag}(L\widehat{\operatorname{Var}}(\hat\beta)L^T)}$.
This checks the contrast mapping, not the statistical assumptions.

```{r matrix-check}
cell_design <- model.matrix(~ 0 + CELL, data = cell_table)
cell_design <- cell_design[, names(coef(fit_clda)), drop = FALSE]
contrast_matrix <- do.call(rbind, weights) %*% cell_design
manual_estimate <- drop(contrast_matrix %*% coef(fit_clda))
manual_se <- sqrt(diag(contrast_matrix %*% vcov(fit_clda) %*% t(contrast_matrix)))
stopifnot(
  max(abs(results$estimate - manual_estimate)) < 1e-10,
  max(abs(results$SE - manual_se)) < 1e-10
)
```

As an independent numerical reference, `nlme::gls()` can fit the same joint
mean model and unstructured covariance. Integer visit indices encode the
original visit positions, including gaps; observations must be ordered by
participant and visit. `corSymm()` supplies unrestricted correlations and
`varIdent()` allows a separate variance at each visit.

```{r independent-check}
long$VISIT_INDEX <- as.integer(long$AVISIT)
fit_gls <- nlme::gls(
  FEV1 ~ 0 + CELL,
  data = long,
  correlation = nlme::corSymm(form = ~ VISIT_INDEX | USUBJID),
  weights = nlme::varIdent(form = ~ 1 | AVISIT),
  na.action = na.omit, method = "REML",
  control = nlme::glsControl(msMaxIter = 1000, tolerance = 1e-8)
)
gls_estimate <- drop(contrast_matrix %*% coef(fit_gls))
gls_se <- sqrt(diag(contrast_matrix %*% vcov(fit_gls) %*% t(contrast_matrix)))
agreement <- data.frame(
  quantity = c(
    "Mean coefficients", "Model-based standard errors", "REML log-likelihood",
    "Planned contrasts", "Contrast standard errors"
  ),
  max_absolute_difference = c(
    max(abs(coef(fit_clda) - coef(fit_gls))),
    max(abs(sqrt(diag(vcov(fit_clda))) - sqrt(diag(vcov(fit_gls))))),
    abs(as.numeric(logLik(fit_clda)) - as.numeric(logLik(fit_gls))),
    max(abs(results$estimate - gls_estimate)),
    max(abs(results$SE - gls_se))
  )
)
stopifnot(all(agreement$max_absolute_difference < c(1e-4, 1e-4, 1e-5, 1e-4, 1e-4)))
knitr::kable(agreement, digits = 7, row.names = FALSE)
```

This agreement validates the mean and contrast estimates, model-based standard
errors, and likelihood calculation to numerical tolerance. It does **not** independently
validate the Satterthwaite degrees of freedom or confidence-interval coverage.

# Assumptions and interpretation

Likelihood-based inference with incomplete responses requires an appropriate
mean and covariance model and an ignorable missingness mechanism, typically
missing at random (MAR) with distinct model and missingness parameters. MAR
allows missingness to depend on observed information; it cannot be established
from the observed responses alone. Including baseline as a response does not
solve missing not at random (MNAR) missingness.

In a real analysis, examine missingness patterns by arm and visit, residuals,
covariance estimates, and convergence diagnostics. Pre-specify sensitivity
analyses for plausible departures from the missingness assumptions. An
unstructured covariance is flexible but can be unstable with many visits
and limited information. Decisions about the model and population should
follow the scientific question, design, and assumptions, rather than which
analysis produces a smaller p-value.
